payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Can the requested paper and cup be identified in the edited image, using the source for context, with sufficient visibility to assess their placement?
node.criteria: Pass if visible features establish the paper and a cup in the edited image and permit assessment of their spatial relation. Fail only if adequate visibility positively establishes that the required paper or cup is absent from the relevant edited scene. Unknown if identity, occlusion, framing, or visibility prevents that determination. Not recognizing a cup is not proof that no cup exists. Report concrete identifying features and visibility limitations; do not judge completion here.
node.binding: Compare source and edited images directly. The source's blue cup provides context, not proof that a reddish object in the edit is a cup. Investigate cup-like opening, interior, walls, and paper boundaries without requiring preservation of the source's color. Do not infer an unseen interior or object identity from the instruction.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image clearly shows a blue printed paper-like item held in a hand. Behind it is a reddish rounded form with a dark curved line, but its visible features do not establish a cup opening, interior, or walls; it could be another object. The source shows a blue cup, but that does not establish the identity of the reddish form. The paper and possible cup are visible enough to inspect, yet the cup cannot be identified with sufficient confidence.

The edited image clearly shows a sheet of paper, but the reddish object behind it is mostly occluded. No cup-like opening or interior is visible, and its visible curved surface alone does not establish that it is a cup. The paper and cup therefore cannot both be identified with sufficient confidence to assess their placement.

A reddish rounded object is partly visible behind it, but its visible features do not establish a cup opening, interior, or walls. The paper is visible, while the cup’s identity and the paper’s placement relative to it cannot be reliably assessed.

response.content: {"text":"The repeated unknowns are valid evidence of an identification/visibility bottleneck, not proof that the requested edit is absent; do not force a “no” from the reference label. The binding already appropriately warns against treating the source cup or instruction as proof of the edited object’s identity. Improve the node’s typed criteria/binding to distinguish observable progress from full placement assessment: inspect the edited image for paper boundaries and cup-specific visible structure, and report whether the paper visibly overlaps, enters, or is merely held in front of the candidate object. Here the paper is clearly visible and overlaps a reddish rounded form, but the form is partly occluded and no opening/interior is established, so placement relative to a confirmed cup remains unresolved. Preserve that uncertainty rather than converting it to absence or completion. Keep source context limited to comparison, and avoid making any single feature (such as a visible interior) an absolute identity requirement when other visible features could establish a cup. No transport, schema, or dependency failures are reported; the issue is semantic ambiguity and insufficient visual evidence, not execution failure."}
